pages.title: A neutral that carries more than the line
pages.for: Loads such as fluorescent lighting banks, rectifiers and drives draw non-sinusoidal current; the three lines' third harmonics add in the neutral, which can then carry more than a line. Table 4Aa says which current sets the cable and by what factor (slides p.33, 34).
pages.rule:
Ibn = 3 × h × IL (h: the third harmonic as a share of the line current)
0 to 15%: line current, factor 1.0
15 to 33%: line current, factor 0.86
33 to 45%: neutral current, factor 0.86
over 45%: neutral current, factor 1.0
It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × the Table 4Aa factor)

Only when the maker's data gives a harmonic figure (slides p.37); say whether it is the third harmonic or THD.
Balanced fundamentals cancel in the neutral; third harmonics add.
No neutral, no neutral current.

traps.text: Expecting no neutral current from a balanced load: true of the fundamentals only.
traps.cite: Slides p.33; IET Wiring Matters 23 (Summer 2007), in research

traps.text: Leaving out the × 3: h × IL is one line's third harmonic.
traps.cite: Slides p.35; IET Wiring Matters 62 (Autumn 2016), in research

traps.text: Sizing on the line current above 33%: at 35% your slides' 150 A circuit has 157.50 A in the neutral.
Leaving out the 0.86 between 15 and 45%, or keeping it above 45%.
Reading a datasheet's THD as the third harmonic without saying so.
traps.cite: Slides p.34; NICEIC on Regulation 523.6.1, in research

pages.where: your slides p.33 to 37; BS 7671 Appendix 4, Table 4Aa, and Regulation 523.6; the Schneider Electrical Installation Guide, sizing the neutral conductor.

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: A balanced three-phase load on a four-wire supply draws 60 A in each line. Its maker states a third harmonic of 35% of the line current. What current flows in the neutral?
pages.alt: 3 × 0.35 × 60 = 63.00 A, more than the 60 A line So the neutral current, not the line current, sets the cable (your slides p.34): 35% is row 3 of Table 4Aa, the neutral current with a factor of 0.86. The slips: 0.00 A is true of the fundamentals alone, which cancel; 21.00 A is one line's third harmonic, 0.35 × 60, and the three lines' third harmonics add.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: A three-phase circuit is normally designed on its line current. Some circuits, supplying rectifiers, variable-speed motor drives or fluorescent lighting banks, draw currents that are not sinusoidal (your slides p.33), and then the circuit may need designing on the [[neutral current]], not the line current (p.34). The On-Site Guide asks the same of a discharge-lighting final circuit: it must carry its [[harmonic currents]] as well as the lamps' current (OSG p.136).
pages.alt: If it is skipped: the neutral current gives rise to additional heating of the cables (IET Wiring Matters 23), and it comes without any matching fall in the line currents (NICEIC, Regulation 523.6.3), so a cable sized on the line current alone does not allow for it.
pages.html: If it is skipped: the neutral current gives rise to additional heating of the cables (IET Wiring Matters 23), and it comes without any matching fall in the line currents (NICEIC, Regulation 523.6.3), so a cable sized on the line current alone does not allow for it.

pages.name: The why
pages.text: At 0% the neutral carries 0.00 A; it passes the 150 A line near a third, and at 35% carries 3 × 0.35 × 150 = 157.50 A.
pages.alt: Your slides' 150 A in each line (p.35), held as the third harmonic grows. Line currents over one cycle L1 L2 L3 0 A 0 A 0 A 120° = one ripple cycle Each line's ripple: all three lie on one wave Neutral: the three lines added at each instant Line, each: 150 A Neutral more than a line Table 4Aa's rows, by third harmonic (%) 0 15 33 45 50 The ripples add to 157.50 A in the neutral, more than the 150 A line, so now the neutral current sets the cable.

pages.name: Which current, which factor
pages.text: Up to 33%, the line current sets the cable (factor 1.0 to 15%, 0.86 above); over 33%, the neutral current (0.86 to 45%, 1.0 above).
pages.alt: Table 4Aa, as your slides give it (p.34). Row 3, 33 to 45%: the neutral is now the larger, so the cable is selected on the neutral current (the Schneider guide; the IET's answer reads "exceeding 33 %"), still with 0.86. YOUR SLIDES P.36 It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × the Table 4Aa factor) The factor goes in with the others. Before a device is chosen, the Schneider guide divides the current that sets the cable by it, giving the design load. No neutral, no neutral current: a three-phase motor often has no neutral connected (your slides p.33).

DBL2's submain is fed three-phase and four-wire, as the course's split of its lighting circuits across L1 to L3 (lesson 2) needs, and most of its load is the key's fluorescent modular and twin fittings. The course takes their third harmonic as 20%, a practice value.

The maker's figure: your slides consider harmonics only when the maker's data states one, and then its percentage goes into these sums (p.37). No datasheet exists for the drawing's own fittings; on the job, no maker's figure means none is applied, so this part shows the method on a practice value. Makers often print total harmonic distortion (THD), which counts every harmonic, not the third alone (a Thorn luminaire datasheet: THD 15.00%), so read which figure the datasheet gives, and say which you used. For scale, IEC 61000-3-2 limits the third harmonic of lighting equipment (Class C) to 30 × the circuit power factor, in percent (Advanced Energy's note). The course applies the 20% to the whole of the heaviest line, L1, though an LED circuit shares it: a cautious simplification, its own.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain why third harmonic currents add in the neutral of a three-phase four-wire circuit, and what that means for the cable.
pages.why: A model answer: In a balanced load the three fundamental currents are 120° apart, so they cancel in the neutral (your slides p.33). The third harmonic runs at three times the supply frequency, so the same 120° between the lines is a whole cycle of it: the three lines' third harmonics are in phase and do not cancel. They add, and the neutral carries the sum of the three lines' third harmonic content, 3 × h × IL (slides p.35). Above about a third of the line current that is more than the line current, so the cable is sized on the neutral current (Table 4Aa, slides p.34 to 36). Above 15% the neutral is also a fourth loaded conductor heating the cable, which the current tables, worked for three, do not allow for, so Table 4Aa applies a factor of 0.86 between 15% and 45%.
